name: Straw man
definition: Distorting a position so that a weaker substitute can be refuted.
example: Christianity teaches three gods, so it contradicts monotheism.
response: Represent the doctrine as one divine essence and three persons before critiquing it.

name: Begging the question
definition: Using the disputed conclusion as a premise without independent support.
example: My interpretation is right because it is the correct interpretation.
response: Ask which premises actually support the conclusion; worldview-level circularity requires further analysis.

name: Ad hominem
definition: Attacking a speaker instead of the relevant argument.
example: Your claim about Isaiah is wrong because you are not a scholar.
response: Test the textual evidence, not the speaker's credentials or character.

name: False dilemma
definition: Treating two alternatives as exhaustive without showing that they are.
example: Jesus must be merely human or Christians must believe in three gods.
response: Identify the omitted alternatives and clarify orthodox Christology.

name: Equivocation
definition: Shifting the meaning of a significant term within an argument.
example: God is one, so there can only be one divine person.
response: Distinguish unity of being from number of persons.

name: Circular reasoning
definition: A conclusion is supported only by premises that depend on that same conclusion.
example: This text is inspired because it is divine, and divine because inspired.
response: Identify the circular dependency; ultimate commitments may be unavoidable but need substantive worldview defense.

name: Appeal to inappropriate authority
definition: Treating irrelevant or insufficient expertise as decisive evidence.
example: A celebrity says the Bible is corrupt; therefore it is.
response: Examine primary evidence and relevant expertise.

name: Appeal to ignorance
definition: Inferring truth solely from the absence of disproof, or falsity from absence of proof.
example: No one disproved this manuscript story, therefore it is certain.
response: Distinguish absence of evidence from positive support.

name: Hasty generalization
definition: Generalizing from a small or unrepresentative sample.
example: One manuscript differs, therefore all Bible manuscripts are unreliable.
response: Evaluate the full manuscript tradition and the variant's significance.

name: Red herring
definition: Introducing an irrelevant issue to divert from the question.
example: Asked about resurrection evidence, the speaker discusses medieval church politics.
response: Return to the original claim.

name: Genetic fallacy
definition: Evaluating a claim solely by its origin rather than its merits.
example: The doctrine was debated at Nicaea, so it was invented there.
response: Check preconciliar sources and biblical exegesis.

name: Tu quoque
definition: Treating an opponent's inconsistency as a refutation of their argument.
example: You also have textual variants, so mine need no examination.
response: Assess both textual traditions independently.

name: Special pleading
definition: Applying a rule selectively without a relevant justification.
example: All ancient reports need scrutiny except my favorite report.
response: Apply consistent evidential standards.

name: No true Scotsman
definition: Arbitrarily redefining a group to evade a counterexample.
example: No real Christian has ever interpreted this differently.
response: Use independent, historically grounded criteria.

name: Composition
definition: Attributing a property of parts to the whole without warrant.
example: Each manuscript is imperfect; therefore the complete textual tradition contains no recoverable readings.
response: Check whether the property transfers.

name: Division
definition: Attributing a property of a whole to each part without warrant.
example: The collection is ancient; every manuscript in it must be ancient.
response: Evaluate individual witnesses.

name: Post hoc ergo propter hoc
definition: Assuming sequence alone establishes causation.
example: A council followed a controversy; therefore it caused the doctrine.
response: Seek evidence for a causal mechanism.

name: Slippery slope
definition: Asserting a chain of serious consequences without adequate support.
example: One disputed reading means all biblical doctrine collapses.
response: Test each proposed implication.

name: Loaded question
definition: Embedding a contested assumption in the question.
example: When did Christians decide to invent the Trinity?
response: Reject the presupposition and ask for evidence.

name: Category mistake
definition: Applying a predicate to an entity of the wrong logical kind.
example: Which divine person is the entire divine essence?
response: Clarify the distinction between person and essence.

name: Affirming the consequent
definition: From P→Q and Q, invalidly inferring P.
example: If inspired, then truthful; this statement is truthful; therefore inspired.
response: Other grounds may explain Q; the inference is invalid.

name: Denying the antecedent
definition: From P→Q and ¬P, invalidly inferring ¬Q.
example: If an autograph, authoritative; not an autograph, so not authoritative.
response: The conditional does not rule out other cases of Q.

name: Undistributed middle
definition: Two categories share a property, but that does not prove membership in each other.
example: All prophets speak of God; this person speaks of God; therefore a prophet.
response: Sharing a predicate does not establish identity of classes.

name: Non sequitur
definition: The conclusion does not follow from the premises.
example: This scroll is ancient; therefore every assertion in it is true.
response: Separate age, accurate transmission, and truth of content.
